title: GDAL 3.13.3
bodyText:
Bug fix release. See release notes: https://github.com/OSGeo/gdal/blob/v3.13.3/NEWS.md

## GDAL 3.13.3

### Port

* Unix file read(): file 3.13.0 regression regarding buffering (#14997, #15005)

### Raster core

* GDALNoDataValuesMaskBand::IReadBlock(): fix memleak in error code path
  (ossfuzz #539042122)

### Raster drivers

COG driver:
 * fix multi-threaded multi-band BuildOverviews() (#15003)

DOQ2 driver:
 * prevent potential int overflow (ossfuzz #538762606)

ENVI driver:
 * fix 3.12.2 regression where multiband BSQ Create/Open fails when band
   offset exceeds INT_MAX (#14968)

GDALG driver:
 * fix nullptr dereference on command_line with space only (ossfuzz #542869626)

GIF driver:
 * Internal libgif: apply security updates of libgif 5.2.2-1ubuntu1.2 of
   Ubuntu 24.04

netCDF driver:
 * Fix subdataset name parsing with multiple colon in path (#14978)

S102/S104/S111 drivers:
 * writer and validator: fix names of dataCodingFormat enumeration (#14985,
   #14998)

ZARR driver:
 * fix nullptr deref on filter id with 'bitround' not in lower case
   (ossfuzz #544518837)

# GDAL/OGR 3.13.2 Release Notes

GDAL 3.13.2 is a bugfix release.

## Build

* CMake: do not attempt find_package(Python) if BUILD_PYTHON_BINDINGS=OFF
  (#14770)
* Build of JP2Grok driver requires libjp2grok >= 20.3.5
* CMake 4.4 compatibility: Remove cmake/modules/CheckCCompilerFlag.cmake,
  CheckCXXCompilerFlag.cmake, CheckLinkerFlag.cmake
* Fix build against Poppler 26.08dev

title: 分析：尼泊尔申请的 2000 万美元"损失与损害"仅覆盖洪灾成本的 0.7%
originalTitle: Analysis: Nepal’s $20m ‘loss-and-damage’ claim only covers 0.7% of flood costs
bodyText: The Nepali government has requested $20m from the UN fund for “ loss and damage ”, following the devastating floods that hit the country in late August. This amounts to just 0.7% of the $2.7bn it has estimated in “physical damage” to infrastructure and “economic losses” from the flooding, according to Carbon Brief analysis. The $20m request would, nevertheless, make Nepal the fourth-largest claimant to the UN loss-and-damage fund, which is intended to help deal with climate-related disasters. Developing countries have already made 176 applications to the UN fund for responding to loss and damage , requesting, in total, $2.8bn to help recover from a variety of damaging events, such as drought, floods and storms. Yet, to date, predominantly developed nations have only pledged $0.8bn to support the fund. This means requests to the fund are already three times larger than the total amount pledged, raising questions about its potential to respond to emergencies. As yet, no funding has been paid out of the fund to developing countries grappling with intensifying and more frequent climate change-induced disasters since it was established in 2023. Nepal’s needs On 26 August, Nepal was hit by flash floods following a catastrophic rock-ice avalanche in the Himalayan border region. The flooding has killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing . Days later, the Nepali government sought an “urgent response” from the board of the UN fund for climate-driven loss and damage. It subsequently requested $20m in “ financial compensation ” from the fund. This is the maximum amount that can currently be requested for a single project. “ Loss and damage ” is a term used to describe how climate change is causing serious and, in many cases, irreversible impacts around the world. Nations established the UN fund in 2023, after decades of effort by climate-vulnerable nations. Nepal’s national disaster management authority has now released an extensive rapid preliminary assessment of “damage and needs” from the floods. As the chart below shows, Nepal’s $20m loss-and-damage claim would only cover 0.7% of what authorities describe as $2.7bn in “total damage and loss” from the floods. When accounting for another $4.8bn in “recovery and reconstruction” costs – part of how loss and damage is internationally defined – then Nepal’s $20m claim would be just 0.3% of the needs it estimates.

title: 解读：海平面上升为何是"人类、遗产与自然的生存威胁"
originalTitle: Explainer: How sea level rise poses an ‘existential threat’ to humans, heritage and nature
bodyText: For millions of people around the world, rising sea levels are already reshaping economies, livelihoods and cultures. The world’s oceans are currently rising at a faster rate than at any time in at least the past three millennia, with human influence the “ dominant cause ” of sea level rise since at least 1970. At the UN general assembly in New York this week, world leaders are set to adopt a high-level declaration on the “existential threats” posed by sea level rise. The declaration notes: “Sea level rise is not a distant scenario, but a real and lived experience for many.” On average, global sea levels rose by 20 centimetres (cm) between 1901 and 2018. This is due to both the melting of glaciers and ice sheets and the expansion of seawater as it warms, as well as changes in land-water storage . The rate of the rise has accelerated in recent years, with ocean levels rising 10.6cm since 1993. Sea level rise can vary locally due to seismic and volcanic activity, groundwater extraction and changes to the Earth’s surface resulting from ice melt. Under a moderate-emissions scenario , scientists predict that global average sea level will rise an additional 56cm by 2100, relative to a 1995-2014 baseline. Here, Carbon Brief unpacks some of the key ways that sea level rise threatens both societies and ecosystems. Cities and coastal communities Biodiversity and coastal ecosystems Small island developing states Coral reefs Heritage sites Cities and coastal communities Biodiversity and coastal ecosystems Small island developing states Coral reefs Heritage sites Cities and coastal communities Around 770 million people – 10% of the world’s population – are at “acute risk” of negative impacts from sea level rise, according to a report from the UN secretary general released last month. (The report defines locations at acute risk as those that are less than five metres above the high-tide line.) The people at risk include the residents of several of the world’s largest cities , including Mumbai and Kolkata in India and Shenzhen and Guangzhou in China. It also encompasses the entire populations of many island nations. (See: Small island developing states .) There are two ways to consider sea level rise. Global-average sea level rise is the amount the ocean surface has moved upwards, on average, relative to a baseline. Relative, or local, sea level rise, is how much the ocean has risen in a given place.

title: 分析：卢拉任内至少保住 2 万平方公里亚马逊雨林
originalTitle: Analysis: Lula presidency saved at least 20,000km2 of Brazilian Amazon since 2022
bodyText: An area of Amazon forest roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey has remained standing due to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s leadership of Brazil, according to Carbon Brief analysis. Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election to become president of the nation that is home to nearly 60% of the Amazon rainforest. Forest loss surged during Bolsonaro’s far-right presidency and dropped sharply under the left-wing Lula, with Amazon deforestation likely to hit its lowest level on record this year. Now, as another presidential election approaches, Lula is facing off against Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro, whose “ anti-environmental ” policies are similar to his father’s. Carbon Brief’s analysis suggests that at least 20,000 square kilometres (km2) of deforestation has been avoided since Lula took office and prioritised Amazon protection. The analysis is based on modelling by an international research team of an alternative scenario in which Brazil’s flagship forest code legislation was not enforced – a proxy for Jair Bolsonaro’s leadership. Experts tell Carbon Brief that this estimate is likely “conservative” and that actual deforestation under Bolsonaro could have been “much higher”. With Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro tied in the polls, the upcoming election is expected to significantly shape the level of environmental action in the world’s fourth-largest emitter, whose emissions are largely driven by deforestation. ‘Brazil is back’ When Jair Bolsonaro was president of Brazil between 2019 and 2022, he championed the nation’s powerful agribusiness sector and oversaw an unprecedented increase in Amazon deforestation. Bolsonaro weakened regulations, slashed federal agency budgets and empowered illegal activities in the Amazon, while attacking Indigenous and environmental groups. This meant that the forest code – Brazil’s flagship legislation that requires landowners to preserve and restore forest on their property – was not properly enforced. After Lula’s presidential victory in 2022, he promised to target “ zero deforestation ” by 2030, telling the COP27 UN climate summit that “Brazil is back”. Lula rolled back Bolsonaro’s wave of deregulation and reinstated a deforestation “ action plan ”. Led by celebrated environmentalist Marina Silva, the environment ministry scaled up enforcement and policing activities in the Amazon. As a result, annual deforestation in the Amazon has more than halved from 11,594km2 per year in 2022 to 5,731km2 in 2025.

bodyText:
Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), implemented by ECMWF — press article, 17 June 2026.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) has expanded its Climate Data Store ( CDS ) with a new suite of datasets. Spanning the atmosphere, land, ocean, cryosphere and water cycle, these additions provide new opportunities to explore how the Earth system is changing and how those changes affect people, ecosystems and infrastructure. Of the new additions to the CDS, some datasets extend climate records further back in time, others deliver sharper regional detail, while others translate climate observations into practical information relevant to topics such as water resources, heat stress and energy systems, helping users better understand the real-world impacts of climate variability and change. Let's take a closer look.

On land, the Global land surface atmospheric variables from 1718 to present from comprehensive in-situ observations dataset offers one of the longest meteorological records available through the CDS. Drawing on observations from weather stations around the world, it provides harmonised and quality-controlled records of key atmospheric variables spanning more than three centuries. The dataset supports investigations into long-term climate variability and change, while also providing an important observational foundation for the development and validation of climate datasets and reanalyses.

bodyText:
Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Climate Bulletin, implemented by ECMWF — published 16 September 2026.

August was the joint warmest month ever recorded globally, with temperatures once again exceeding 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels

August 2026 was the joint hottest month on record worldwide, tied with July 2023, as reported in the latest Climate Bulletin by Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) 1 . The month also saw the average sea surface temperature (SST) over the extra-polar ocean – between 60°S and 60°N – reach a record high. This new record can be explained by global heating from burning fossil fuels and rapidly increasing SSTs in the equatorial Pacific, which were associated with strong El Niño conditions.

Global-average surface air temperature (°C) for 2023 (orange), 2024 (yellow), and 2026 (dark red). All other years between 1940 and 2025 are shown with grey lines. Data source: ERA5. Credit: C3S/ECMWF.

Globally, the average surface air temperature in August was 16.96°C, making it the hottest month ever recorded (for all calendar months), tied with July 2023. Notably, this temperature was 1.65°C higher than the estimated 1850-1900 pre-industrial baseline for the month, putting the world once again over 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. The last time this value was exceeded was less than a year ago, in November 2025. Additionally, it was the warmest August ever recorded, surpassing the previous joint August record, which was set in 2023 and 2024.

The month marked the end of the world's joint hottest June to August period on record, tied with 2024. August also saw the end of western Europe's warmest summer ever recorded, which exceeded the previous long-standing record set in 2003. Western Europe's summer was marked by a succession of intense heatwaves across the region – a sequence that began exceptionally early and continued throughout the season.

title: FLEX and Sentinel-3C launched
bodyText:
FLEX and Sentinel-3C launched — ESA / Applications / Observing the Earth, 15/09/2026.

Flight VV30 lifted off on 15 September at 03:21 (14 September at 22:21 local time).

A launch adapter called Vespa allowed both satellites to be stacked inside the Vega-C fairing for launch. Positioned on top of Vespa, Sentinel-3C was injected into orbit first, followed by FLEX approximately one hour later.

Following the satellites’ separate deployments, ESA’s European Space Operations Centre in Germany received the all-important first signal from each satellite, confirming that both had been safely released from the rocket and had established contact with ground control.

Mission controllers will now spend the coming days conducting the ‘launch and early orbit phase’, meticulously checking and verifying the health and performance of both satellites and confirming that all systems are functioning as expected.

ESA’s Director of Earth Observation Programmes, Simonetta Cheli, said, “Today’s launch is the culmination of years of scientific innovation, engineering excellence and international cooperation.

“Developed within ESA’s FutureEO programme, FLEX is a research mission that will advance our understanding of plant health and the role of photosynthesis in the carbon and water cycles. Sentinel-3C is the third satellite in the Sentinel-3 series, systematically measuring Earth’s oceans, land, ice and atmosphere to support Europe’s Copernicus Services.

“Preparing and launching two satellites together is no easy task. My thanks go to the many experts who have contributed throughout both satellites’ development, testing and preparation for launch, and who have worked tirelessly to ensure that both satellites have reached orbit safely.”

FLEX to reveal the hidden activity of Earth’s vegetation

FLEX, the latest Earth Explorer mission, is ESA’s first satellite designed specifically to measure photosynthetic activity from space. Its Fluorescence Imaging Spectrometer will detect the extremely faint fluorescence emitted by plants as they absorb sunlight during photosynthesis.

EOGS will comprise satellites, ground infrastructure, data and information, processing facilities, and distribution infrastructure. EOGS will also draw on commercial services, the sharing of Member States’ own capacities and complementary core capacities developed specifically for and owned by the EU.

This true-colour image of the Venetian Lagoon in northern Italy was acquired by the IRIDE satellites on 17 May 2026. It shows the city of Venice, with its distinctive Grand Canal curving through the historic centre, surrounded by the blue waters of the lagoon and a number of islands.

Venice came to prominence as a maritime republic and seafaring continues to be an important part of the city’s identity, as well as a key form of local transport. The white trails left by boats are clearly visible in some of the busy waterways around the lagoon – including on the south side of the city, near the Murano islands to the north and the Vignole islands to the east.

As well as its famous canal networks, the lagoon’s landscape also includes mud flats, salt marshes and shallow tidal waters. Sediment suspended in the water causes parts of the image to appear bright blue, while the dark blue is where the water is clearer. The sea is a darker shade of blue in the lower-right corner of the image, where Venice Lido, with its white-sand beach, borders the Adriatic Sea.

bodyText: LGBTQ+ refugees have fled persecution across East Africa in search of safety. In South Sudan’s Gorom Refugee Settlement, many say that the violence and harassment have followed them By Kate Plummer When Amy arrived in South Sudan’s Gorom Refugee Settlement, she hoped she would finally be offered protection after three volatile years. The 31-year-old transgender woman had left Uganda in 2021, fearing persecution. She had questioned her sexual and gender identity from a young age but had grown up in a conservative religious family in a country with harsh anti-homosexuality laws. She felt muzzled. If you tell people about your sexuality, ‘your head is chopped off, anything can happen’, she said. Amy’s growing fear about her future in Uganda came to a head when, aged 18, her family caught her with her male netball coach, whom she had started dating in secret. Scared, she ran away, eventually reaching a refugee camp in Kenya before moving to Gorom when proposed anti-LGBTQ+ legislation threatened to upend her life again. But for Amy and other LGBTQ+ people in Gorom, refuge has brought little security. Life remains a daily struggle against discrimination, hate speech, verbal harassment, intimidation and targeted attacks because of their sexualities and gender identities. Gorom Refugee Settlement lies 26 kilometres southwest of Juba, South Sudan’s capital. The camp, built in 2010, is under the authority of the South Sudanese government through its Commission for Refugee Affairs and is supported by several organisations, including UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, the Red Cross and Peace Winds. It was originally intended to house 2,500 refugees fleeing conflict in Ethiopia, but it’s now overflowing. According to a UNHCR spokesperson, some 16,000 refugees live in the settlement and on 22 June this year, the camp stopped registering new arrivals. The spokesperson declined to say how many of the refugees are LGBTQ+, citing confidentiality. Amy estimated the number at around 600. Image: LG Graphics Amy is one of several LGBTQ+ refugees who told Geographical about being beaten at night, attacked at water collection points and harassed by other refugees because of their sexual and gender identities. Some of the refugees, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, also said their businesses had been burnt down and that neighbours had sent them letters demanding that they leave the camp.

bodyText: Rory Walsh explores South London’s Victorian vision of prehistoric Britain Southeast London. August lately over, and a new Prime Minister sitting in Downing Street. Implacable summer weather. As little mud on the ground as if the waters had but wholly retired from the face of the earth, and it’s wonderful to meet a megalosaurus, ten metres long or so, gazing like an elephantine lizard on Sydenham Hill… Almost 175 years after Charles Dickens wrote the opening of Bleak House, a walk through Crystal Palace Park today invites the above reworking. Dickens imagined a megalosaurus crawling unnoticed through winter mud in his version. The one I’m looking at, a stern green giant with sharp teeth and hunched shoulders, stands proudly on display after Britain’s driest summer. The megalosauruses are among the biggest of the Crystal Palace Park dinosaurs. The 30 or so statues, built just after Bleak House was published, were the world’s first life-sized models of extinct animals. When they were unveiled to the public in 1855, the dinosaurs were a sensation. Besides visual spectacle, they were intended to educate Victorian visitors about the emerging science of palaeontology. The statues were placed in a carefully landscaped Geological Court. Winding footpaths still lead around three scenic islands set within a tidal lake. The islands represent scenes from the Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras, with the statues chronologically arranged to create a ‘walk through Deep Time’. Alongside them, a set of ‘Geological Illustrations’ showcases Britain’s geological and mineral resources. Massive amounts of quarried rock were transported to the park from across the country, including Yorkshire, the Peak District and the Dorset coast. A bridge overlooks a reproduction stratified cliff, complete with geological faults and a thick seam of coal. Elsewhere are artificial outcrops of chalk and sandstone. Initially, the site had a replica lead mine. The statues themselves were made in plaster from clay moulds. The larger ones are lined with enough material to build a house. An iguanodon, for example, contains 600 bricks, 900 tiles and more than 30 metres of iron framework. Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins, the noted sculptor who cast them, consulted the latest research to decide what creatures may have looked like. Exquisite details include the complex eyes of the ichthyosaurs and layered fur on the giant ground sloth.

title: Galileo achieves first-ever civil authenticated GNSS position using Signal Authentication Service (SAS)
bodyText:
European GNSS Service Centre (GSC) news, 17 September 2026.

On 16 September, Galileo achieved a major milestone in satellite navigation resilience by demonstrating the first-ever civil GNSS position authenticated through both navigation data and ranging information. The demonstration used the Galileo Signal Authentication Service (SAS) concept, with five Galileo satellites transmitting encrypted signal components over Europe. Receivers on the ground successfully processed these signals to compute an authenticated position fix, demonstrating a new level of protection for civil satellite navigation.

On 16 September, between 14:00 and 16:00 UTC, five Galileo satellites—E06, E21, E23, E34 and E36—encrypted one of their signal components, the E6-C signal at 1278.75 MHz, normally transmitted in the clear. Several Galileo SAS receivers deployed at different locations successfully processed these signals in combination with Galileo Open Service Navigation Message Authentication (OSNMA) . For the first time, a civil GNSS receiver was able to process authenticated navigation data and ranging measurements from at least four satellites simultaneously and compute an authenticated position fix.

A significant part of the demonstration took place during Jammertest on the island of Andøya, Norway, where controlled GNSS jamming and spoofing tests are conducted using real over-the-air signals. This provided a unique opportunity to evaluate Galileo SAS under both nominal conditions and many types of spoofing.

During the spoofing tests, conventional receivers were deceived and reported false positions, while the Galileo SAS receiver detected the attack and maintained a trusted position solution based on authenticated Galileo signals.

Historically, civil GNSS receivers have had limited means to verify that the signals they use genuinely originate from navigation satellites. Galileo addressed part of this vulnerability through OSNMA, declared operational in 2025, which authenticates the navigation data transmitted by Galileo satellites. SAS complements OSNMA by protecting the other fundamental source of information used to compute a GNSS position: the ranging measurements.

bodyText: We the undersigned write this letter out of great fear and great hope. Over the last few months, we’ve seen the world set ablaze by both war and warming. From the conflict in Iran, which has claimed thousands of lives and disrupted billions more, to the series of ever worsening climate disasters, from wildfires in Europe to collapsing glaciers in Nepal, the world seems to be falling apart exactly when it needs to be coming together. We know that these crises are connected. The oil that governments fight over is also the carbon pollution that is warming our climate. The bad air quality in Delhi, the high price of fuel in Vietnam, the cost of electricity in the United States, the terrifying floods in the Himalayas – they all connect back to fossil fuels. Until we end that dependence, we’ll never be able to address the climate emergency and stop fighting these endless oil-soaked wars. That’s why today we are inviting the world to unite around a common cause: repowering the world with cheap, clean energy. We are calling on governments, businesses, institutions and the public to work together to provide clean, affordable energy to everyone, everywhere by 2030. From the nearly 1 billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more of us who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels. We know this world is within reach. Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most. With cheap solar, wind and batteries, we can create huge and rapid change. California is already using just half as much natural gas to generate electricity as it did three years ago, thanks to solar and batteries. In Pakistan, people have put up millions of solar panels in just months, relying on social media for instruction. Each month, millions more people across sub-Saharan Africa are getting electricity for the first time with home solar kits. This energy transition is already moving quickly – but we need it to go much quicker. And so we come together to urge two steps. First, we must build clean power for everyone. For the first time ever, we can reliably bring electricity to the one in 10 people on earth living without regular access. We ask everyone who can afford it to donate something so that others can turn the lights on for studying, cooking and medical care – and never have to think about a gallon of diesel or gas again.

bodyText: warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions of a super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high. The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger . Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February , from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating. While the weather system develops in the Pacific Ocean, its knock-on effects will be felt far away. It increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world, while increasing rainfall elsewhere. India has already experienced a 50% shortfall in essential monsoon rains this month, affecting crops. In Sri Lanka, reservoirs for drinking water are running dry. European countries may be indirectly affected, with a stormier autumn, but the primary impact for them is likely to be on food supplies . Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary. It is beyond doubt that the effects of this natural phenomenon are compounded by human-made folly and injustice. Domestically and internationally, the poorest will be worst hit, due to factors such as living conditions and underlying health, while being the least able to pay their way out of trouble. originalTitle: Country diary: A tangle of butterflies and battle re-enactments | Paul Evans
bodyText: I ’m telling the story from a pub in the bailey opposite the ruins of Oswestry Castle. There in 1165, Henry II, the Angevin (Anglo-Norman) king of England, gathered troops from the Marcher Lords to advance on an alliance of Welsh princes for control of the Marches. The previous Sunday, 861 years later, we went the same way as Henry’s army to Chirk Castle , Castell Y Waun a’r Ardd, to see a re-enactment of the Battle of Crogen . The present castle wasn’t built back then and the battle at Crogen was in the Ceiriog Valley below. Henry had sent woodsmen to raze woodland in the valley to remove the Welsh advantage, but he left one oak, Quercus petraea , at which Owain Gwynedd gathered his army. That tree became the Pontfadog oak – a giant, the oldest British oak, and survived as the National Tree of Wales, much loved and storied until it blew down in a storm in 2013 at an estimated 1,600 years old. I have a small fragment of it given to me by the longtime Guardian environment editor John Vidal . A small copper butterfly. Photograph: Bob Eade/Butterfly Conservation/PA The battle re-enactment, with crashing swords and shields in the colours of Marcher lords and Welsh princes, fine horses and boinging arrows, was fun to watch with a running commentary giving a sense of what was happening and who was doing what. Histories vary about whether this was a great battle, isolated harassments or no fighting at all, but the outcome was the same: the Welsh won. The history of the Marches, like the traumatised, ghost-ridden ground itself, has been a contested space for centuries. It was fascinating to talk to people dedicated to making the past come to life for modern audiences. Over the castle garden wall, the past and present were weaving together in micro-dramas of moment. Two clouded yellow butterflies, Colias croceus , which had migrated here from north Africa or southern Europe, were flickering over herbaceous borders and lawns. Given the massive decline in insect populations, that pastoral scene had a spirit of resistance. And as if to demonstrate a mystical kind of heraldry and valour of a far more ancient territorial warrior, a small copper , Lycaena phlaeas , flourished his wings. bodyText: MCDERMITT CALDERA, Ore.—On a cold and overcast spring morning, Katie Fite stood in one of the country’s last sage-grouse strongholds, contemplating the wooden stakes in the ground that she fears warn of its destruction. Every spring, males of the chunky bird species with spiky tail feathers come to a dwindling number of locations to strut, pop their inflatable white neck pouches and make a “ paloop, paloop ” sound in an attempt to court a mate. As their name suggests, sage-grouse need sagebrush, the green-brown shrub that once dominated arid Western landscapes. But both the bird and its habitat are rapidly disappearing due to climate change, invasive species, wildfires and energy development. Now a mining company wants to extract lithium here. A greater sage-grouse flies through the Warner Mountains of Oregon. Credit: John Carlson/USFWS Millions of sage-grouse once filled the West, but federal data shows their numbers have plummeted 80 percent since 1965 as more than a million acres of the sagebrush landscape they depend on is lost every year. They’ve long teetered toward the endangered-species list . “We want to save sage-grouse?” Fite, public lands director for WildLands Defense, asked as she walked through the mating area, known as a lek, on the public lands where the McDermitt Lithium project would dig. “This is not how we do it. This is a travesty.” The project’s owner agreed to avoid drilling during the sage-grouse breeding season in an effort to avoid impacting a species that is easily put off mating if conditions aren’t just right. But there is so little sagebrush habitat left in the country, Fite said, that “you can’t even pretend to mitigate this.” Today, the U.S. has only one operating lithium mine—Albemarle’s Silver Peak in Nevada. By 2030, at least six new mining projects are predicted to be extracting lithium from American soil and another 13 will soon follow, according to a database compiled by Columbia Journalism Investigations and Inside Climate News. Scores more are proposed, their wooden stakes marking companies’ claims. This element of the energy transition—lithium is used in batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage—poses stark dilemmas in the communities atop the so-called white gold. Mining it uses and displaces water, and much of it is found in water-scarce regions. Tribal nations repeatedly harmed by past extraction are disproportionately located on or near lithium-rich lands. And then there’s vulnerable wildlife.

bodyText: On a clean summer swell, the wave at Malibu’s Surfrider Beach arrives from the south, wraps around a cobblestone point and unspools toward the pier in a long, shimmering wave that can carry a surfer for hundreds of feet. It breaks slowly, forgivingly, over rounded stones that were delivered by Malibu Creek across millennia. The beach plays an outsized role in American and surf culture, inspiring the films “Gidget” and “The Endless Summer” and the songs of the Beach Boys. The point produced the longboarding style that still bears the place’s name: In Australia, longboards are called “Malibus.” Kassia Meador has been reading this wave for nearly 30 years. She was 15 the summer she first paddled out at Surfrider Beach, and she has spent the decades since becoming one of the most recognizable longboarders in the world. She calls it, without hesitation, the best wave on the planet. Lately, when Meador paddles out, something is missing beneath her: the beach. The sand at Surfrider Beach has thinned to the point where, at high tide, the ocean reaches almost to the Pacific Coast Highway. The wave itself has changed shape; the three distinct points that made Malibu’s Surfrider Beach have collapsed into one, she said. “It bunches everybody together,” she said. There’s more crowding and more tension in the water, and less of the wave that made the place worth protecting. What’s happening at Malibu is about human intervention—a century of dams, seawalls and paved-over rivers that have starved this coastline of the sediment that builds its beaches. But it is becoming a climate story, fast, because a coast stripped of its natural defenses is a coast with nothing left to absorb what’s coming. And what’s coming this winter is a lot. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center has an El Niño Advisory in effect and puts the odds of a very strong event this fall and winter at greater than 90 percent —it recently broke the highest surface temperature recorded for this phenomenon, months before the projected peak. California Governor Gavin Newsom declared a statewide emergency on Monday in anticipation of heavy rainfall, high waves and flooding the phenomenon could bring. Malibu’s First Point is one of 57 surf breaks a team of scientists, working with the conservation group Save the Waves, assessed in a study published this year in the journal Climatic Change.

bodyText: Daniel Swain has made a name for himself studying the extremes of a warming planet. Fires, floods, droughts, heat, storms: if it’s a record breaker, Swain has probably studied it. As a weather and climate research scientist at UCLA’s Institute of the Environment and Sustainability , Swain has dedicated his life to understanding so-called “outlier events” and how climate change is super-charging them. Then, he explains them, and not just to fellow scientists. He devotes over 1,000 hours a year to climate communication for the public. Swain is the mind behind “Weather West,” and coined the term “Ridiculously Resilient Ridge ” in December 2013, as a first year graduate student, for the high pressure ridge perpetuating the 2011-2017 northern California and Pacific Northwest drought. As a climate scientist, and life long Californian, he has been keeping a close eye on the current El Niño. Based on a recent study in Science , the current El Niño is likely the strongest in over a millennium. Following this revelation, the U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres warned, "The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up." Officials from Britain to Los Angeles are issuing advisories for residents to prepare and stock up on essentials in preparation for this historic El Niño. In a recent interview, Swain and Inside Climate News reporter Nina Dietz discussed why this El Niño is unlike anything we’ve seen before, and what it could mean for California and beyond: DANIEL SWAIN: So El Niño is a recharge oscillator, which is effectively a battery. The tropical oceans are a big heat sink. The tropics are warm, there's a lot of sun directly on the water, and then the currents subduct some of that heat to deeper layers. But then, you reach a point where there's so much energy in the Pacific that it becomes unstable, and the system needs to equilibrate. The way it does that is through an El Niño. Climate scientist Daniel Swain. Credit: Courtesy of Daniel Swain This is why El Niño and La Niña, the El Niño Southern Oscillation or ENSO collectively, is semi-cyclical, coming around every two-seven years or so. That's something you can take to the bank. We can view it as a battery, because there is a certain point beyond which it's not going to continue to overcharge. So El Niño is the ocean system discharging a full battery. We're going into extreme territory with this one, probably record breaking.

title: 热成像揭示极端高温的"隐形不公正"：欧洲今夏至少 3 万人死亡
originalTitle: Revealing the Invisible Injustice of Extreme Heat
bodyText: The extreme heat scientists have warned about for decades came to Europe again this summer, killing at least 30,000 people like a silent, invisible plague. It came for poor people, the very young and very old, and those suffering from debilitating conditions. The final toll will likely be higher. A 2024 United Nations report estimated about 175,000 annual heat-related deaths across Europe, and total deaths in European Union countries spiked above 60,000 in 2022 and 2024. The heat started earlier than ever, in late May, and kept coming in deadly, unrelenting waves that destroyed crops and vineyards, buckled railroad tracks, turned forests to kindling and dried up rivers and lakes. When it settled heavily over Bologna, Italy , in late June, residents of the industrial region said it was like a stifling, life-threatening force that you feel in your bones, transforming streets and buildings into radiators blasting warmth day and night, making routine outdoor chores dangerous. Heat is hard to see, but you feel it in the pavement, in the walls of poorly insulated apartments, in sweat that never quite dries and a bedroom that just won’t cool down. And people do not experience it equally. Bologna photographer Michele Lapini made those differences visible, using his iPhone and a thermal sensor to document temperatures in homes, workplaces and public spaces as the heat gripped the city. The images show that construction workers in direct sun, delivery riders crossing the city and residents of old apartment buildings and poorly cooled senior centers inhabit radically different thermal worlds than people with access to air conditioning, shade and well-insulated homes. Piazza Maggiore was between 93 and 103 degrees Fahrenheit at 9:28 p.m. during the “Il Cinema Ritrovato” festival, promoted by the Cineteca di Bologna. Federico, 56, works as a meteorologist; a few years ago, he invested his savings to improve his apartment’s energy efficiency using renewable energy, keeping the temperature around 70 degrees Fahrenheit at 5:48 p.m. Michele, 31, works as a metalworker and lives in a rented apartment on the same floor as Federico’s, but without any energy efficiency upgrades or air conditioning. His apartment was above 90 degrees Fahrenheit at 5:57 p.m. Lapini said he felt a great sense of resignation as he talked with people about the heat. What could they do? They had no choice but to work. They couldn’t move or get a permit to install air conditioning, or afford it.

bodyText: The world has spent a decade trying to put a price on nature, yet the criminal economy has been putting a price on it for much longer. Land grabbing, illegal logging, illicit gold mining and wildlife trafficking are extremely lucrative and have become a serious drag on both sustainable development and climate action, a new op-ed argues, and its drivers must be addressed from where extraction begins all the way to corporate offices. “The world is still working out how much a standing forest is worth. Criminal markets settled on a price for a felled one long ago,” the authors write. This article is a commentary. The views expressed are those of the authors, not necessarily of Mongabay. The world has spent a decade trying to put a price on nature. Forests have become carbon sinks, while wetlands are increasingly described as natural infrastructure. Biodiversity is also being drawn into financial markets. Governments and investors have poured billions into carbon markets and conservation finance, including green bonds. Around them, a financial system is emerging on the assumption that intact ecosystems can generate enough economic value to protect them. A more destructive economy has been putting a price on nature for much longer. It makes money by extracting and selling it. Land grabbing, illegal logging, illicit gold mining and wildlife trafficking are usually treated as environmental offenses, so responsibility falls to park rangers, customs officials and specialized police. That view badly underestimates what is happening. In a new paper for the Brookings Institution, we argue that environmental crimes are a serious drag on both sustainable development and climate action. They damage ecosystems and weaken the institutions charged with governing them. They also drain revenue from legitimate companies and public coffers. Enforcement alone will not solve a problem that runs through trade, finance and local political economies. An IBAMA agent participates in a raid on an illegal logging and mining operation within an Indigenous reserve. Image courtesy of IBAMA. Global criminal economy No one knows exactly how large this economy has become. A widely cited estimate puts annual proceeds at between $110 billion and $281 billion, but the true figure is probably far higher, perhaps in the trillions. What makes the business so difficult to see is that much of the money disappears into transactions that look perfectly ordinary.

bodyText: OTAGO PENINSULA, Aotearoa New Zealand — Sandfly Bay was long a key nesting area for yellow-eyed penguins ( Megadyptes antipodes ), noisy, pink-footed birds that spend long days foraging at sea. But this wild beach on the Otago Peninsula, like others nearby, has gone quiet. In 2024, the last breeding-age female at Sandfly Bay, who’d been consistently producing chicks for a dozen years, drowned in a fishing net. Fishing has been one of many factors driving the species, which is only found in Aotearoa New Zealand, toward extinction. In the 2008-2009 breeding season, there were 739 breeding pairs in the “mainland” New Zealand population, which includes pairs on nearby islands. But the population has dropped since then to 117 pairs — a decline of more than 80%. These figures don’t account for yellow-eyed penguins on New Zealand’s remote southern islands, which are poorly surveyed. The IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority, listed the species as endangered in its last assessment, in 2020, when the mainland population was still twice what it is now. Several experts told Mongabay that the species’ chances of survival are slim, though most said they still had faith. “I think I’d always like to say that there’s hope because otherwise why do you do what you do, but things are pretty dire,” Trudi Webster, a marine scientist who’s worked on research and conservation of the species for the past decade, told Mongabay. A number of organizations are working to save the yellow-eyed penguin, and much of the conservation concern has centered on set-net fishing. Set nets act as a vertical wall anchored in the water that catches fish by their gills or entangles them. They’ve drowned numerous yellow-eyed penguins. Over the objections of fishers, the New Zealand government recently opted to make a set-net closure around the Otago Peninsula permanent and set an annual fishing-related mortality limit of four penguins. Conservationists say it’s not enough. A yellow-eyed penguin lingers between the trees and the beach at a nesting site in Moeraki managed by Penguin Rescue. Image by Edward Carver for Mongabay. A treasured species, a multitude of threats Yellow-eyed penguins are an iconic species in New Zealand, appearing on the $5 bill and drawing tourists to Otago. Stuffed yellow-eyed penguins even greet travelers at the airport in Dunedin, the area’s main city.

Greenland is capped with a vast ice sheet that spans 1.7 million square kilometers (656,000 square miles) and measures more than 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) at its thickest point. Below all this ice lies a landscape human eyes have never seen directly. But a newly developed method for mapping this hidden bedrock has produced the most detailed and accurate view of it yet.

The new map reveals an expansive network of valleys carved into the surface beneath the Greenland Ice Sheet. Many of the features formed well before most of the ice above them existed, offering new context for the island’s geologic history—and potentially helping scientists refine projections of the ice sheet’s future. Scientists described the newly mapped valleys in a NASA-led paper published in Geophysical Research Letters .

Satellites map the ice surface in fine detail, and scientists can use these subtle bumps and dips to infer the shape of the landscape buried below. The work aims to improve future versions of BedMachine Greenland , a high-resolution dataset of the terrain beneath the ice sheet.

FIM produces estimates of land area covered in water based on model forecast river flows and current conditions that predict where flooding impacts may occur in the following days. It’s a tool for forecasters, emergency managers and the public that alerts users to the latest river and stream flooding conditions.

“Inundation maps are a critical tool for assessing the impacts of flooding,” said NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs, Ph.D. “NOAA prioritized expanding FIM to ensure that nearly every American can access detailed information beyond the expected river crest height. These maps further support NOAA's mission to protect lives, safeguard property, and strengthen our national economy.”

FIM puts river and stream flooding on the map at a neighborhood scale. It depicts flooding potential along 3.3 million river miles throughout the continental U.S., U.S. territories and Hawaii. title: What’s in a name? Naming things in OpenStreetMap
bodyText:
Almost everything has a name and OpenStreetMap volunteers have mapped 115 million names .

In OpenStreetMap, the verbal identifier with which people refer to something is documented by the name= tag. This usually is the most common name in the local language and is the most obvious name of the feature. For example, if you are in France and map a road called “Rue des Beaux-Arts”, you add name=Rue des Beaux-Arts so that everyone knows what that road is called.

There are many map styles based on OpenStreetMap data. On www.openstreetmap.org , we display “osm-carto” style by default, with a layer switcher for many others.

There are a few simple rules that the OpenStreetMap community follows, including:

name= is typically the commonly used name in the local language. A street in Paris has as name= its French name, not the name in English.

name= should be a proper name – not a description or a reference id.

originalTitle: Cities across the world are sinking because of groundwater depletion, but the process can be reversed
bodyText: Land subsidence, the gradual sinking of the ground surface, affects many of the world's major cities. Parts of Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia, are sinking more than 10 centimeters (4 inches) each year, prompting the government to plan a relocation of the city. The coastal city of Tianjin, China, is home to 15 million people. It, too, is a subsidence hotspot. If sinking there continues unabated, 15% of the city could be at risk of flooding by 2050. Groundwater depletion is the main driver: when water is pumped from aquifers, the pore pressure that supports the overlying sediment drops and the ground compacts.

bodyText: As a powerful nor'easter hit the U.S. Atlantic coast in late September 2026, the ocean poured into coastal neighborhoods from North Carolina to New York. Water from the storm surge and heavy rain filled streets and surrounded homes as near-hurricane-force winds knocked out power. Storm surge is the piling up of water caused by strong winds pushing water onshore. There are four basic factors that determine the surge height at any given location: the strength of the onshore wind, the size of the storm, the shape of the coastline and the depth of the ocean. The September 2026 surge was highest where the water was directed into shallow bays and inlets. Some of the largest surges during the nor'easter were in Raritan Bay in New Jersey and Delaware Bay. The slow movement of the nor'easter up the East Coast resulted in a large, sustained surge. A computer model forecasts the nor'easter's winds in late September 2026. Credit: Brian Tang, NOAA images.

bodyText: Ice cores recovered from an ice cap in northwestern Tibet appear to preserve fragments of ancient ice from the last ice age, extending Earth's glacial record by more than 100,000 years and making them the oldest ice cores ever recovered from the region, according to a new study. The analysis, comparing ice cores drilled from the Guliya Plateau in 1992 and 2015, shows that both samples contained similar oxygen isotope patterns, suggesting that the environmental signals they contain are consistent and reproducible. Researchers take samples from the Guliya Plateau inside of a core drilling dome in 2015. Credit: The Ohio State University. To measure the true age of the ice, researchers employed advanced dating techniques to detect two radioactive isotopes, beryllium and chlorine. The team used these elements to mark the Laschamp geomagnetic excursion, more than 41,000 years ago. Outside of the polar regions, this is the only ice core we have from the mountaintops that goes back that far, Thompson said.

title: 全球供应链中断情景下中国原油贸易网络的韧性研究
bodyText: 《地理研究》45年第10期（第演化经济地理栏目，2878-2900页，DOI 10.11821/dlyj020241176，网络首发 2026-09-29）。全球供应链中断情景下中国原油贸易网络的韧性研究。摘要：原油贸易网络的研究通常缺乏对外部事件冲击下网络近实时自组织动态调整过程和韧性特征的探讨，本文基于船舶原油贸易流量数据，构建了2019—2021年间中国原油贸易近实时网络，并运用复杂网络的韧性βeff模型和“V型”曲线，分析2020年由全球疫情导致的供应链中断场景下，中国五大港口群参与的原油贸易网络的自组织动态调整过程及其韧性特征。研究发现：① 中国原油贸易网络整体韧性处于中等水平：尽管港口群全球贸易对象港口数量从216减少至193，网络的连边数和平均度有所降低，但2021年贸易量与2019年基本持平。② 五大港口群呈现不同的韧性表征：环渤海港口群通过新增与阿曼、新加坡和科威特等国的贸易量以提高韧性应对疫情冲击；长三角港口群减少与沙特阿拉伯、伊拉克和阿曼等国的进口，转而加强与韩国、巴拿马和美国等国的合作；珠三角港口群则主要通过增加来自沙特阿拉伯、安哥拉和伊拉克等国的进口来提高韧性；东南港口群的贸易韧性较弱，至2021年底未能恢复到疫情前水平；西南港口群由于贸易量较少，未显著受到疫情冲击。③ 本研究采用的韧性βeff模型有效补充了传统网络指标对韧性的表征：环渤海港口群和长三角港口群展现出较强的网络自适应调整能力。本研究结果为中国原油贸易在突发事件冲击下的合作关系调整和航线布局优化提供了理论和实证支持，同时为保障中国原油安全提供了重要的战略指导。

title: 陇中黄土丘陵区乡村社会网络结构特征及其韧性演化机制——以秦安县郭嘉镇为例
bodyText: 《地理研究》45年第10期（第乡村地理栏目，3062-3087页，DOI 10.11821/dlyj020250681，网络首发 2026-09-29）。陇中黄土丘陵区乡村社会网络结构特征及其韧性演化机制——以秦安县郭嘉镇为例。摘要：乡村社会网络是乡村组织依托多元社会关系相互联结形成的关系结构，其韧性表现为网络在外部扰动下维持功能连续，并通过结构重组实现从吸收、恢复到适应的综合能力。本文以秦安县郭嘉镇为例，基于问卷调查与访谈数据构建乡村社会网络，分析不同发展阶段乡村社会网络的结构特征及其演变趋势。在此基础上，采用节点强度与中介中心性识别关键支撑节点，并结合全局效率衰减与网络崩溃阈值测度网络韧性，模拟随机失效与定向攻击情景下的网络响应机制。研究结果表明：① 乡村社会网络由内聚型“单中心+双核”向多中心格局演进，并逐步形成“多中心-多层级”的虚实耦合结构；② 节点韧性呈核心-边缘分异，中心村庄、集市与县城构成强韧核心；③ 网络韧性表现具有情景依赖性，随机失效下传统阶段占优、城镇化阶段最低，定向攻击下信息化阶段优势突出；④ 韧性演化本质是“结构-功能-政策”相互作用的动态耦合过程，推动乡村联结实现由同质凝聚向有机连接的适配性转型。

title: 黄土区坡面水土保持措施对流域水沙关系的影响
bodyText: 《地理研究》45年第10期（第自然地理栏目，2786-2801页，DOI 10.11821/dlyj020251019，网络首发 2026-09-29）。黄土区坡面水土保持措施对流域水沙关系的影响。摘要：植被梯田等坡面水保措施已显著改变了黄土区景观。针对坡面水保措施是否改变流域水沙关系这一问题，选择坝库修建较少的祖厉河流域（黄丘五区）、天水站（黄丘三区）和西峰站（黄土塬区）进行了研究，研究时段从20世纪50年代至今。在天水站和西峰站，尽管流域治理减沙率高达60%左右，但仍重现了前期研究在晋西离石站（黄丘一区）的结果，即水沙关系不变、含沙量不变、减水率和减沙率接近。在祖厉河，流域治理减沙率高达82%，但60余年来日尺度水沙关系保持不变，洪水期含沙量始终为645±5% kg/m3。与天水站和西峰站不同，祖厉河的年水沙关系发生了变化，主要是由于治理后流量减幅太大，以至于小流量且低含沙量的组分显著增加。在黄土区，流量低于某一阈值后含沙量才衰减，因此只有当流域治理达到相当程度、流量减至该阈值以下时，才会诱发含沙量的降低，使得减沙效率激增，这为黄河产沙锐减提供了新的解释。研究结果表明，尽管黄土区植被和梯田建设导致“山川巨变”，但日或事件尺度的流域水沙关系保持不变。这意味着对以坡面治理为主的流域，洪水期或极端降雨下仍会出现与治理前相同的高含沙量，减沙仅通过减洪实现，因此减沙率可直接用减洪率估计，这对解决植被梯田减沙效益估算这一难题具有重要意义。

title: 乡村人口收缩与耕地规模化转型协同关系的空间异质性及影响因素——以陕西省为例
originalTitle: 乡村人口收缩与耕地规模化转型协同关系的空间异质性及影响因素——以陕西省为例
bodyText: 基于2010—2020年人口普查、社会经济等数据，本文采用空间分析方法探究陕西省县域乡村人口收缩-耕地规模化转型协同关系的空间异质性，并遵循规模经济与农业生产适宜性理论思想构建解释框架，采用最优参数地理探测器和模糊集定性比较分析（fsQCA）法识别其影响因素及作用路径。研究表明：① 陕西省多数县域在乡村人口收缩背景下实现了耕地规模化转型，2010—2020年全省乡村人口收缩-耕地规模化转型弹性系数（协同性）为10.73%。② 2010—2020年，乡村人口收缩-耕地规模化转型同步区零星分布于各市；耕地规模化转型超前区主要集中于陕北黄土高原区北部、汉中盆地以及西安-商洛交界地带；滞后区呈现轴带格局，主要位于关中平原内部。

bodyText: 管理提质 服务增效 为推进乡村全面振兴提供坚实水利支撑贵州省深入学习贯彻习近平总书记关于“三农”工作和治水的重要论述，以及巩固拓展脱贫攻坚成果、推进乡村全面振兴的重要指示批示精神，按照水利部统一部署，着力提升脱贫县水利管理服务水平，持续为推进乡村全面振兴提供好水利支撑保障。一、纵深推进河湖长制，为“和美乡村”提供良好水生态层层压实五级河湖长责任，动态调整河湖长名录，建立涉河湖重大问题调查处置机制，深化与周边5省市联防联控联治。常态化开展河湖库“清四乱”，完成5万余个遥感图斑核查、3万余个问题整改，对1059条河流系统开展健康评价。持续指导脱贫县聘请和发挥好河湖保洁日常巡查保洁作用，既带动群众就近就业增收，又守护好群众身边的水清岸绿。二、持续深化运行管理，为“宜居乡村”提供坚实水安全积极推行农村供水“3＋1”标准化建设和管护模式，因地制宜建立县级统一管理为主，区域专业管理、村级组织管理为辅，村民自用自管为补充的山地供水运行管理模式，45个脱贫县基本实现县域统管，稳定发挥工程效益。通过轮训和举办技能大赛，持续提升2.5万名管水员业务能力。编制发布农村供水保障宣传画册、保障服务水平质量倡议书和节水护水抗旱倡议书，推动形成全社会爱水、惜水、护水良好氛围。推进水利工程标准化管理，制定重大水利工程投融建运改革实施意见，开展湄江水库现代化运行管理矩阵试点，系统提升水库综合效益。完成水库、堤防管理与保护范围划定，对脱贫县1668座水库、2088公里堤防开展白蚁隐患普查和治理，消除安全隐患。三、强化节约集约利用，为“宜业乡村”提供精细水服务全面落实水资源刚性约束，将管控指标纳入省对市县考核，健全农业节水增效 “五项制度体系”，深化龙里、息烽农业用水权改革试点，实现脱贫县1147个非农规模以上取用水户、35个重点中型灌区在线计量全覆盖。全面推行水资源费改税，建立水利与税务跨部门联动机制，2025年水资源税达6亿元；持续提升服务效率，首创AI智能审查和“云勘验”模式，实现20分钟完成38项指标审查、30分钟核发证照；推进用水权市场化交易，累计完成38单、0.6亿立方米交易，帮助乡村特色产业解决用水难题，让水资源成为助力乡村产业发展的“活水源头”。四、拓展水利劳务帮扶，为群众增收创造增长点深入贯彻落实促进农民持续稳定增收的工作部署，发挥好水利工程点多面广优势，持续扩展水利劳务帮扶。每年聘请脱贫人员或低收入人员约1100名从事小（2）型水库日常管理，通过“一卡通”系统每人每年发放1万元报酬。常态化聘请7000余名群众从事农村供水管水员，月均工资600元。水利工程累计吸纳农村劳动力就业6.26万人次，发放工资8.29亿元，在224个水利工程推广以工代赈，带动1.2万名群众就近务工，发放劳务报酬1.68亿元，水利建设成为助力乡村振兴的“增收工程”。（根据贵州省有关材料整理）滴水穿石开新局 水润云岭惠民生“十四五”以来，云南省坚决落实巩固拓展脱贫攻坚成果同乡村振兴有效衔接部署，对标“两不愁三保障”及饮水安全核心要求，始终把饮水安全作为乡村振兴民生底线，把国家乡村振兴重点帮扶县作为水利帮扶重中之重，以水破题，用心用情用力书写全省乡村振兴水利篇章。一、倾斜投入，筑牢重点帮扶县水利根基云南省共有国家乡村振兴重点帮扶县27个。针对其自然条件恶劣、水利基础薄弱、工程性缺水突出的实际，省水利厅在资金、项目、政策、技术上持续加大倾斜力度。“十四五”以来，累计向27个国家重点帮扶县投入水利建设资金93.34亿元，其中，中央资金89.64亿元、省级资金3.70亿元，为重点帮扶县破解水困、夯实发展根基提供了坚强保障。

title: 青海海西州发生5.1级地震 水利部迅即启动水利抗震救灾调度指挥机制
bodyText: 本站讯 2026年9月4日1时4分，青海省海西州直辖区发生5.1级地震，震源深度10千米。水利部迅即启动水利抗震救灾调度指挥机制，召开专题会商会，分析地震对水利工程和农村供水影响，研判震区雨水情形势，安排部署水利抗震救灾工作。水利部根据全国“水利一张图”，迅即排查震区河流湖泊以及水库、水电站、堤防、水闸、农村供水工程、水文测站等分布情况，并及时通报青海省水利厅，指导督促地方水利部门抓紧摸排震区水利工程震损情况，加强中小河流和山洪灾害监测预警，落实水库安全度汛措施，保障震区群众生命、饮水安全。据预报，震区未来三天有小雨。水利部将密切关注震区雨情、水情及水利工程运行情况，指导地方水利部门继续做好震区水利工程震损排查和群众饮水安全保障工作，严防发生次生灾害。

title: 李国英赴西藏调研冰湖监测预警及风险防范工作
bodyText: 李国英调研普钢落错冰湖本站讯 9月3日至6日，水利部党组书记、部长李国英在西藏调研冰湖监测预警及风险防范工作时强调，要深入学习贯彻习近平总书记重要指示精神，按照党中央、国务院决策部署，坚持人民至上、生命至上，树牢极限思维、底线思维，抓紧开展青藏高原冰湖调查，全面排查摸底风险隐患，强化动态监测预警，提高灾害链风险研判和识别能力，建立健全上下游风险隐患监测预警和响应联动机制，落细落实防范链式灾害风险责任和措施，切实维护人民群众生命财产安全和社会大局稳定。李国英调研错高堰塞湖治理和监测工作李国英先后来到西藏墨脱县、米林市、工布江达县，详细了解冰湖分布、类型、监测预警及风险防范等情况，并深入尼洋河支流巴河边浪曲源头查勘普钢落错冰湖及其下游错高堰塞湖、老虎嘴水库等，与有关负责同志和技术专家研讨冰湖监测预警和链式灾害风险识别与防范应对措施。李国英调研尼洋河支流巴河边浪曲河道李国英指出，青藏高原冰湖分布广、数量多，且多位于江河源头。受全球气候变化影响，溃泄风险不断累积，风险暴发往往引发链式灾害，严重威胁下游安全。要全面摸清青藏高原冰湖情况，充分利用高分卫星遥感、无人机载雷达等现代化监测手段，科学布设水文、地震动仪等监测设施，以及坝体位移形变、渗流渗压、应力应变等智能传感设备，构建“天空地水工”一体化的综合监测感知系统，精准掌握冰湖发展变化，及时预警溃泄风险。李国英强调，要坚持系统观念，以流域为单元，深入分析冰湖溃泄的致险、承险、防险要素，充分考虑各环节风险链式叠加放大效应，“一湖一策”“一河一策”制定防范应对方案。要建立健全上下游风险隐患监测预警和响应联动机制，落细落实链式灾害风险防范各环节各方面责任和措施，增强“时时放心不下”的责任感和“事事心中有底”的行动力，确保人民群众生命财产安全。

bodyText: 本站讯 据预报，受南海热带低压影响，9月13日至15日，海南将有大到暴雨，其中海南南部将有大暴雨；南渡江、昌化江、万泉河将出现明显涨水过程，暴雨区内部分中小河流可能发生超警以上洪水。依据《水利部水旱灾害防御应急响应工作规程》，水利部于9月13日10时针对海南启动洪水防御Ⅳ级应急响应。指导督促地方水利部门密切监视南海热带低压影响态势，强化雨水情监测预报，及时发布预警信息，科学精准调度骨干水库拦蓄洪水，突出抓好中小水库安全度汛、山洪灾害和中小河流洪水防御

sourceName: SpaceMapper 资讯（中文航天与对地观测转载层）
title: 24小时欧洲航天动态：织女星-C双星发射升空，多项目稳步推进
bodyText:
北京时间2026年9月15日9时21分，欧洲在法属圭亚那库鲁航天中心的ELV发射台，由意大利Avio公司研制的织女星-C（Vega C）小型运载火箭执行VV30发射任务，采用瞬时发射窗口点火升空，整个发射与载荷部署过程持续近2小时，最终按计划将欧洲空间局（ESA）的Sentinel-3C与FLEX两颗卫星送入预定的太阳同步轨道，任务取得圆满成功。

本次任务的轨道参数为倾角98.6度、轨道高度约810公里，这一轨道设计能够让两颗卫星对全球地表实现全覆盖观测，且可以保证卫星每日在同一地方时经过同一观测地点，为长期连续的地球环境监测提供稳定的轨道条件。根据任务流程，火箭起飞后55分28秒，AVUM+上面级完成第二次点火，在起飞后1小时00分49秒，重1143千克的主载荷Sentinel-3C率先完成分离；在起飞后1小时56分03秒，重397千克的FLEX卫星完成分离。载荷部署全部完成后，火箭上面级进行第五次点火，执行末级离轨处置操作，主动再入大气层焚毁，全程符合欧洲空间碎片减缓规范，避免产生长期滞留轨道的太空垃圾。

Sentinel-3C是ESA哥白尼计划（Copernicus Programme）Sentinel-3卫星家族的第三颗卫星，由泰雷兹阿莱尼亚航天公司（Thales Alenia Space）研制。作为欧洲全球环境与安全监测体系的核心组成部分，Sentinel-3系列卫星承担着海洋、陆地、大气多要素综合观测的职能。此前该系列的Sentinel-3A、Sentinel-3B卫星分别于2016年、2018年从俄罗斯普列谢茨克航天发射场，采用基于SS-19洲际导弹改装的Rockot运载火箭发射升空，目前已在轨运行超过8年和6年，逐步进入寿命后期。

Sentinel-3C与后续待发射的Sentinel-3D将承担起任务接续的职责，把Sentinel-3系列的连续观测数据记录延伸至2030年代，为全球气候变化研究、海洋生态监测、灾害应急响应、农业估产等领域提供长期稳定的数据源。该卫星搭载的标准化仪器套件，包括海洋和陆地表面温度辐射计、海洋颜色成像仪、合成孔径雷达高度计、微波辐射计等，可实现对海平面高度、海表温度、海洋水色、陆地植被覆盖、湖泊水位、极地冰盖变化等参数的高精度观测，是目前全球地球观测体系中不可或缺的组成部分。

本次任务搭载的FLEX（Fluorescence Explorer，荧光探测卫星）同样由泰雷兹阿莱尼亚航天公司建造，是ESA“地球探索者”计划的第八颗科学卫星，其核心载荷为Floris荧光成像光谱仪。该仪器能够捕捉到植物光合作用过程中释放的肉眼不可见的太阳诱导叶绿素荧光信号，这一信号直接反映了植物的实际光合效率与健康状态，突破了传统遥感仅能观测植被覆盖度、叶面积指数等表观参数的局限。

FLEX卫星入轨后，将与Sentinel-3系列卫星形成编队观测，结合Sentinel-3提供的温度、植被指数等同步数据，科学家可以精准反演全球不同生态系统的植被胁迫状况，比如干旱、高温、病虫害对农作物和森林的影响，量化陆地生态系统的碳汇能力，进一步明确植物光合作用在全球碳循环、水循环中的作用，为气候变化模型优化、农业生产管理、生态保护政策制定提供关键的科学数据支撑。

title: 大同火山群文旅热度持续攀升，奔赴火山脚下的“诗和远方”
bodyText: 作为世界唯一发育在黄土高原上的火山群，大同火山群国家地质公园拥有三十多座形态各异的火山锥，被誉为“东亚大陆稀有的自然遗产”“火山地质博物馆”。近年来，这片地质瑰宝跳出单一观光模式，研学科普、星空露营、田园赏花、乡村民宿多点开花。走进火山群景区，狼窝山环形木栈道盘旋火山口边缘，游客缓步穿行，近距离观察火山锥、火山岩等地质遗迹。串联火山群、黄花基地、桑干河湿地的精品旅游线路热度攀升，实现“观光+研学+休闲+度假”一体发展。

title: 科普月趣探科学！广州青少年科技馆周末活动预告（9月12日-13日）
bodyText: 浩瀚深海蕴藏着丰富的能源资源，是人类未来重要的资源宝库。本次活动将由广州海洋地质调查局ROV技术室副主任，高级工程师张亚念带领大家解锁深海秘境，认识海底各类珍贵能源资源，了解海底资源的分布特点与开发价值。活动时间：9月12日（星期六）14:30-16:00（签到时间：14:00-14:30）。活动对象：40组5-12岁少年儿童及家长（一大一小），同一家庭限报一场。报名方式：点击推文左下角“阅读原文”进入报名系统；或关注“科普广州”公众号，回复关键词“科学课”获取报名链接，名额有限，先到先得。

bodyText: 详情：2026年以来，为有效净化网络环境，安徽滁州网信、宣传、公安等部门持续深化网络谣言治理，切实维护网络空间秩序和人民群众合法权益。现公布5起打击整治网络谣言典型案例：案例1：网民陈某为博取眼球，编造发布“听到两声巨大的爆炸声，有人说是飞机掉下来了”的不实信息。案例2：网民赵某发布视频并配文“洪水防汛荒草圩二圩又要炸圩喽”，造成不良影响。经核实，相关言论系谣言。

title: 四川宜宾高县连发三次地震，有居民称凌晨被震醒后和家人躲厕所避险，当地：正排查灾情
bodyText: 9月26日，四川宜宾高县连发三次地震。据中国地震台网消息，5时1分，高县发生4.5级地震；5时8分，高县发生3.4级地震；7时57分高县发生4.4级地震，震源深度均在5至6公里左右，震中位置接近。据四川地震局消息，地震发生后，四川省地震局迅即启动四川高县4.5级地震四级应急响应。此次4.5级地震烈度为4至5度。震中距珙县9公里、距高县16公里、距叙州区24公里、距宜宾市27公里。高县应急局工作人员告诉记者，有专职工作人员统计相关灾情情况，目前他未收到相关情况。

sourceName: 澎湃新闻·滚动新闻
title: 澎湃新闻即将推出2026国庆特别策划《奔赴“县”场》
bodyText: 县城，盛得下梦想，载得动乡愁。一到假期，年轻人“奔县”已成为一种风潮。今年国庆，澎湃新闻记者也将奔赴“县”场，感受蕴藏于中国县域的生机、韧性与真实生活。这里既有县域产业突围、文旅融合的鲜活探索，也有古老文脉在小城焕发新生的转型实践，用一个个小城故事，描摹新时代中国基层的生动图景。县域活则全盘活，县域强则根基稳。一段时间以来，各地县域经济你追我赶、百花齐放、竞相发力，持续释放经济发展活力，在产业体系建设和促进就业等方面发挥了重要作用。大国发展的脉搏，就藏在数千座县城的街巷、产业与人声之中。中国旅游协会发布的《2026年上半年旅游市场洞察报告》显示，上半年，县域旅游成为市场重要增长极，“宝藏小城”“奔县游”热度持续攀升，县域异地消费同比增长14.1%。来到县城，许多游客觉得更具烟火气、更有“活人感”。小城文旅怎样打开发展新天地，焕发长久生命力？在一个个县域样本中，发现一个别样精彩的中国。县城，是烟火气蒸腾的地方，是干事创业的所在。这组报道以实地走访为底色，记录县域产业活力、城乡变迁、普通人的选择与坚守，摒弃刻板印象，多维度呈现县域发展的机遇与活力。从烟火民生到个人故事，从文化传承到基层治理，于细微处触摸中国式现代化的肌理。今年年初以来，澎湃新闻连续推出以县域经济为观察视角的策划报道《小城，何以生机勃勃》和《单项冠军县，何以扛打》，图文、视频合计发稿超过80篇。这些策划通过“小城”这一独特视角，生动诠释了中国经济的韧性、活力与多元动力，为理解中国基层社会的真实发展状态提供了宝贵的新闻报道文本。国庆假期也是观察县域经济活力与特色的重要节点 ，为此澎湃新闻再推策划《奔赴“县”场》，读懂中国经济发展的深层动力。设计：祝碧晨

sourceName: 澎湃新闻·滚动新闻
title: 上海古镇｜新场：浦东最大的“活着的古镇”
bodyText: 上海的古镇，是江南水乡的璀璨遗珠，亦是海派文化的源头沃土。截至目前，上海共有11个古镇入选中国历史文化名镇——新场、高桥、川沙、朱家角、练塘、金泽、枫泾、张堰、嘉定、南翔、罗店。2025年，上海首次为本市历史文化名镇专门立法；2026年3月《上海市历史文化名镇保护条例》正式施行。2026年9月，专为上海11座名镇制作的《上海古镇画报：11座中国历史文化名镇精华》正式发布（可点击阅读报道，文末有下载链接）。本系列以该画报为蓝本改编而成，带您走近上海11座中国历史文化名镇，一览它们的深厚底蕴和现今风采。今天介绍的是浦东规模最大、历史遗产最丰富的历史文化名镇——新场。如果你想在上海找一座最像江南梦里的古镇——小桥流水、老宅深巷、家家枕河——那一定不能错过新场。新场，古称“石笋滩”，成陆于唐代中期，因旧盐场南迁而得名。元代盐业兴盛，新场渐铸为重镇，现为浦东规模最大、历史遗产最丰富的历史文化风貌区。2008年，新场获评“中国历史文化名镇”；2019年，作为上海唯一代表，与江浙12个古镇携手申报“江南水乡古镇”世界文化遗产。新场现存12万平方米历史建筑，保留“十字街、井字河”的水乡格局与“前店中宅、跨河后花园”的宅院布局。西式建筑毗邻而立，马头墙、观音兜等传统建筑元素随处可见，中西合璧之韵流转街巷。张氏宅第石库门雕花精细，拱券、罗马柱、彩窗点缀其间；第一楼书场评弹声声；南山古寺内两株700年银杏，静默守望历史兴衰。新场与上海国际旅游度假区、上海野生动物园构成浦东中部“文旅黄金三角”。周边有大治河公园、浦江郊野公园环抱，近可拐入王桥村，感受田园意趣。古镇非遗琳琅满目：浦东派琵琶弦音铮铮，锣鼓书说唱铿锵，江南丝竹悠扬；“三月廿八”庙会上，龙舞小戏轮番上演；卖盐茶、灶花、土布、三角粽、木雕，透着生活温度；新凤蜜露水蜜桃栽培、绞圈房营造技艺，见证农耕与建筑智慧。交通：上海地铁16号线至新场站，转乘公交可达；自驾可从S20外环高速、S2沪芦高速沪南公路出口沿导航抵达。以上插画包括20余个推荐的新场代表性游览点。这些游览点既有不可移动文物、历史建筑，也含乡土风物、原生商号、老字号，还包括新时代的文创、特色场景，和当地招牌美食。千年积淀，凝于几处角落。以下着重介绍新场五个必打卡的文化地标，每一处都值得驻足细品。新场第一楼书场——洪福桥畔的百年“第一高楼”，听一曲评弹品一杯清茶第一楼书场始建于清同治末年，20世纪20年代翻建为三层楼房，时为镇上高度第一，故称“第一楼”。其一层有临河廊道，建筑特色鲜明，地理位置优越，楼下即是洪福桥。登楼临窗，听评弹声声，看桥下流水——这是新场最江南的打开方式。新场信隆典当——新中国故宫博物院首任院长学徒旧地，18元读懂千年新场信隆典当始建于清末，时为典当行。故宫博物院首任院长吴仲超曾在此做学徒十载。现为新场历史文化陈列馆，既是了解新场历史文化的窗口，也是红色文化和江南文化的展示点。参观费用为18元/人。一家典当行，走出故宫掌门人，也藏着一部新场史。千秋桥——浦东体量最大的古石拱桥，月夜登桥赏“千秋夜月”千秋桥原名“仗义桥”，清康熙年间建，是浦东体量最大的古代石拱桥。其东22级、西21级台阶，桥身高广。曾有新场“石笋十景”之一“千秋夜月”，指的就是月夜登上千秋桥，上下一色的美景。新场海派中医文化基地——在张小乙宅里，看中西合璧建筑与海派中医的相遇新场大街中段矗立着一幢古色古香的小楼——张小乙宅。作为海派文化的一个缩影，张小乙宅兼容了中式、日式、西式等多元建筑风格。现为新场海派中医文化基地，由新场镇政府和上海市中医文献馆于2022年共同打造。建筑本身就是展品，中医文化在此新生。南山雅集——古镇南入口的“首站文化空间”，雅集、展览、沙龙轮番上演南山雅集为新场古镇南入口“首站文化空间”。其定期举办各类传统文化雅集、艺术展览、学术沙龙及高端文创展示等活动，为市民游客提供品味古镇文化底蕴、体验当代雅致生活的文化会客厅。走进南山雅集，便是走进了新场的文化客厅。江南水乡，千年新场。 下次去上海野生动物园或迪士尼，记得拐进这座浦东最大、最完整的千年古镇——在十字街与井字河之间，有一座活着的江南水乡在等你。有关新场古镇的更多介绍，请扫描以下二维码查阅。扫描下方二维码，下载《上海古镇画报：11座中国历史文化名镇精华》。

title: 国庆假期上海两大机场预计日均客流42.8万人次，同比增长5.5%
bodyText: 2026年国庆假期将至。9月29日，澎湃新闻记者从上海机场集团获悉，假期期间，上海浦东、虹桥两大机场预计共保障航班起降1.7万架次，同比增长3.7%，其中浦东机场1.2万架次、虹桥机场0.5万架次；保障进出港旅客300.2万人次，日均42.8万人次，同比增长5.5%，其中浦东机场195.2万人次、虹桥机场105万人次。值得一提的是，国庆节当天，浦东机场将携手上海科技馆在2号航站楼国内混流层揭幕亚洲最大长须鲸骨骼标本展。据上海自然博物馆公开资料显示，该长须鲸骨骼标本长达24米、重约3吨。长须鲸是仅次于蓝鲸的世界第二大动物，而该长须鲸于2017年3月20日被一名渔民在上海市浦东新区老港镇附近海域发现搁浅在滩涂边，随后由上海自然博物馆标本制作团队耗费22天将鲸就地完成分解后运送回馆，并历时4年，最终将其制成骨骼标本。此外，记者从上海市公安局浦东分局获悉，国庆期间，通往崇明、启东方向的G40长江隧道预计将迎来车流峰值。据预测，9月30日至10月7日，隧道进出城总车流预计达90.8万辆次，日均通行量约11.4万辆次。其中，9月30日10时起，长江隧道出城方向将率先迎来通行高峰，出现车流缓行现象；10月1日为出城流量峰值日，单日车流约8.6万辆，较2025年同期上涨2.4%；返程最高峰在10月6日，当日进城车流约7.8万辆，较去年同期小幅下降1.3%。假期期间，G40沪陕高速长江隧桥将实施黄牌货车限行政策，限行时段为9月30日12时至10月1日22时、10月6日至7日每日8时至22时。

sourceName: 澎湃新闻·滚动新闻
title: 奔赴“县”场｜安徽黟县：如何从“到此一游”到“留此成邻”
bodyText: 县城，盛得下梦想，载得动乡愁。一到假期，年轻人“奔县”成风潮。今年国庆，澎湃新闻记者奔赴“县”场，感受中国县域的生机、韧性与真实生活。这里既有县域产业突围、文旅融合的鲜活探索，也有古老文脉在小城焕发新生的转型实践。今天，我们关注安徽黟县。我们坐车从黄山北站出来，沿新铺的旅游公路往黟县碧阳镇石亭村走。路旁指示牌上依次写着“西递”“宏村”“碧山”。每个指示牌背后，都是全国知名的景区与旅游目的地。县城不过七万多本地人，一年却接待1900多万外地游客。走访里，我们深刻感受到一套文旅产品正在这个小县城悄然迭代：从“看房子”到“做鱼灯”，从“到此一游”到“留此成邻”。黟县，或许能为中国县域文旅经济提供一种样本。
